A premium bond’s coupon is not all return: plan for the amount paid above face value

Use four graphics to distinguish coupon rate, current yield and annual cash-flow yield, then trace a separate reserve intended to replace a nominal premium gap at maturity.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 4 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Compare hypothetical bond rates and a nominal-capital reserve

Interactive planning lab

Annual coupon rate on face value6.00%
Current yield: annual coupon divided by purchase price5.45%
Annual-coupon cash-flow yield to maturity4.72%

Original hypothetical nominal-CAD bond illustration. A fixed non-callable bond is bought immediately after a coupon at the entered price, pays one annual coupon at each year-end and repays face value at maturity. All issuer payments are assumed honoured. The cash-flow yield is the effective annual discount rate equating these annual receipts with the purchase price; it is not a dealer’s semiannual or day-count quote conversion, a forecast or a guaranteed realised compound return. The separate reserve target is the positive difference between purchase price and face amount, with no inflation allowance. Equal reserve deposits are made at each year-end after prior reserve cash earns the selected return. That reserve return is assumed after its own tax and costs, while bond coupons and redemption are shown before bond tax and transaction costs. If the reserve deposit exceeds the coupon, outside cash is required to fund the illustrated plan; no borrowing or extra money is silently supplied. Calculations retain fractional cents; actual payment rounding would change a final adjustment. No interim bond valuation, early call, default, accrued interest, tax treatment or fee is calculated.

The central idea

A bond bought above face value repays less principal than its purchase price at maturity. Spending every coupon and preserving the original nominal capital are different cash plans.

01

Read the price and the face amount as different numbers

The Investor.gov premium definition describes a bond priced above its par amount. The purchase price is what the buyer pays; the face amount is the principal due at maturity under the assumed payment terms.

The default example has CAD 10,000 of face value but costs 110% of face, or CAD 11,000. It pays an annual coupon equal to 6% of face: CAD 600. If held to the assumed ten-year maturity with all payments honoured, its final principal receipt is CAD 10,000, not CAD 11,000.

The example is non-callable and purchased immediately after a coupon, so it contains no accrued-interest payment, early redemption or market sale. It models an original set of terms rather than quoting an actual bond.

02

Give each rate its own definition

The coupon rate divides the annual coupon by face value: CAD 600 ÷ CAD 10,000 = 6%. Current yield instead compares the annual coupon cash with the purchase price. CAD 600 ÷ CAD 11,000 is about 5.45%.

The annual-coupon cash-flow yield to maturity also accounts for the dates and amount of the principal repayment. It is the annual discount rate that makes the present value of ten CAD 600 coupons plus CAD 10,000 at year 10 equal CAD 11,000. The modeled rate is about 4.72%.

SEC’s corporate-bond bulletin discusses price, coupon and yield to maturity as separate terms. Here the yield solves annual cash flows in effective annual units. It is not a calculation of an investor’s realised compound return when coupons are spent or reinvested at a different rate.

03

Choose whether the cash plan is intended to preserve nominal capital

Suppose the household wants the original CAD 11,000 available at maturity before the excluded bond tax and transaction costs. The expected face repayment supplies CAD 10,000, leaving a nominal capital gap of CAD 1,000.

That gap is not a bill sent by the issuer during the holding period. It is the difference between the selected future capital target and the principal expected back. Setting money aside to fill it is a separate saving decision that reduces the coupon cash available for other spending.

The tool funds only a positive premium gap. If the bond is bought at face value or a discount, no premium reserve is required by this particular nominal target. The example does not estimate an inflation-adjusted capital target.

04

Trace the reserve deposits rather than deducting the whole premium from one coupon

At the default assumed 2% annual reserve return after its own tax and costs, equal year-end deposits of about CAD 91.33 grow to CAD 1,000 over ten years. The annual coupon less that reserve requirement is about CAD 508.67, before bond tax and costs.

The reserve calculation divides the premium gap by the future-value factor for equal year-end deposits: ((1 + reserve return) raised to the years − 1) ÷ reserve return. At zero return, that factor is simply the number of years, so the CAD 1,000 gap requires CAD 100 a year over ten years.

The reserve line assumes those deposits are actually made. If a low coupon or short maturity makes the required deposit larger than the coupon, the waterfall becomes negative. The difference would need outside cash; the model does not assume a loan or create that funding.

05

Compare ending capital beside the consumption that was forgone

If all coupon cash is spent and no reserve is built, the modeled capital retained at maturity is the CAD 10,000 face repayment. A fully funded default reserve adds CAD 1,000, producing CAD 11,000 before the excluded bond tax and costs.

The second case has consumed less coupon cash along the way. Its higher ending capital is therefore not an increase in the issuer’s coupon or a free investment gain. The separate reserve’s growth also depends on the independently assumed return.

The matrix varies the price premium and reserve return while retaining face value and maturity. It calculates an amount to set aside, not a probability of success or an assessment that a replacement investment will provide the assumed return. The coupon affects the ability to fund the reserve, even though it does not determine the size of the premium gap.

06

Keep the coupon budget, return calculation and risk review separate

A rate calculation cannot establish that the issuer will pay, that a sale before maturity will recover the price paid or that tax and transaction costs are negligible. Those matters are outside the matched cash-flow illustration and need the actual terms and records.

The related call-risk guide shows how an issuer’s early redemption can stop coupons before the expected date. The bond-goal guide considers needing cash before maturity. Either change would require a different cash calendar from the fixed schedule used here.

For a household plan, record the expected coupon cash, the amount reserved for any selected capital target and the amount available after the applicable costs and taxes. The coupon percentage, current yield and cash-flow yield help describe the bond, while the spending and reserve decisions determine where its cash goes.
